entry.title: Two Engines, One Server - Inside InternLM/lmdeploy

link.title: Two Engines, One Server - Inside InternLM/lmdeploy

entry.content:
LMDeploy from the InternLM team at Shanghai AI Laboratory occupies an interesting spot in the inference landscape. It ships two independent inference engines — a pure-PyTorch engine you can read and hack like any research codebase, and TurboMind, a C++ and CUDA engine whose benchmark numbers were deemed strong enough to earn a EuroSys 2027 paper — and hides the choice behind one async engine interface and one OpenAI-compatible server.

That dual-engine design is what makes the repository worth a slow read. The Python side under lmdeploy/pytorch shows exactly how paging, continuous batching, and fused mixture-of-experts kernels are expressed in modern PyTorch and Triton, while the native side under src/turbomind shows the same problems solved with a hand-written scheduler and architecture-specific kernels. Above both sits a serving layer that speaks OpenAI and Anthropic protocols and a proxy that fans requests across multiple model instances. Licensed under Apache-2.0, the project supports far more than InternLM checkpoints: DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, Llama, and a growing list of vision-language models all run through the same paths. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The overview shows the fork in the road: one async engine that delegates to either the readable PyTorch engine or the compiled TurboMind core, depending on the backend you pick at launch.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The unified CLI parses every subcommand — chat, serve, convert — and maps arguments onto engine configuration.
  • The lite toolkit calibrates a model on sample data and produces AWQ or GPTQ quantized checkpoints before deployment.
  • The OpenAI API server is a FastAPI app that accepts chat-completions requests and streams tokens back over SSE.
  • Request shapes are defined by protocol models, which also carry usage accounting for token billing dashboards.
  • The async engine is the heart of the serving layer: it queues requests, forms batches, and forwards them to whichever backend was selected.
  • Inside the PyTorch engine, the model agent — the largest Python file in the repo at over 1,700 lines — manages device buffers, cache updates, and forward passes for every step.
  • The CUDA kernel library implements paged attention, KV cache filling, and fused MoE in Triton and PyTorch.
  • On the native side, the TurboMind scheduler plans prefill and decode waves, honoring priority policies and KV memory limits in about 1,400 lines of C++.

Why You Need This

Throughput on commodity GPUs is the first reason. TurboMind’s kernels are tuned per GPU architecture — the linear attention kernels for Hopper-class cards are one example of that attention to silicon — and the project has published strong MoE and mixed-precision numbers on hardware as ordinary as V100-class cards. If you serve open models to real users from rented GPUs, the difference between engines is measured directly in your monthly bill, and having both engines behind one switch means you can benchmark on your own traffic instead of trusting someone else’s chart.

The second reason is the serving surface. The async engine exposes OpenAI chat-completions plus an Anthropic adapter, so clients written for either hosted provider keep working when pointed at your own box. The model proxy goes a step further: it can front several model instances at once, which turns a single deployment into a small routing layer for A/B testing two models or spilling overflow traffic from a small model to a big one.

The third reason is educational symmetry. Because both engines exist side by side, you can read the paged attention kernel in Python one hour and the C++ scheduler the next, comparing how each handles the same batch-scheduling decisions. The prefill scheduler in the PyTorch engine and its C++ counterpart make the same trade-offs — admission control, chunked prefill, block accounting — in two languages, which is a rare and honest way to learn serving systems.

The detail graph separates the six layers: CLI, serving and API, the PyTorch engine, the TurboMind native stack, the quantization toolkit, and the vision-language wrapper.

Trace a request from the top. The CLI dispatches serve into the API server, which validates the payload against protocol models and hands it to the async engine. A session manager keeps interactive chat history resumable across reconnects. The engine’s backend switch — the two edges labeled engine=pytorch and engine=turbomind in the diagram — is the whole architectural story: identical request state flows into either implementation.

On the PyTorch side, the engine loop advances batches and hands per-session streaming to engine instances. The model agent is where the interesting memory work happens: it builds positional and block tensors through the inputs maker, writes new keys and values via fill_kv_cache, and dispatches attention to the right backend — standard paged attention for most models, MLA for DeepSeek-style latent attention. Model definitions such as deepseek_v2.py wire expert routing to the fused MoE kernel.

On the TurboMind side, a checkpoint converter rewrites Hugging Face weights into the native tensor layout before the pybind bridge instantiates the C++ engine. The scheduler owns admission and wave planning, consulting a prefix trie to reuse shared prompt caches, and the largest CUDA file in the tree — moe_utils_v2.cu — implements the gather, scatter, and GEMM helpers that expert routing needs.

From Install to a Running Server

A working GPU box with recent CUDA drivers is enough to start. Install with pip install lmdeploy, then launch a terminal chat with lmdeploy chat internlm/internlm2_5-7b-chat — the CLI pulls the checkpoint from the Hugging Face hub, converts weights on first run, and starts streaming. For an HTTP service, run lmdeploy serve api_server internlm/internlm2_5-7b-chat and point any OpenAI-compatible client at port 23333. Useful dials at launch include --tp for tensor parallelism across GPUs and --cache-max-entry-count to cap how much VRAM the KV cache may claim. For quantized deployments, run the lite flow first: lmdeploy lite calibrate followed by lmdeploy lite auto_awq produces a compressed checkpoint that both engines load directly.

Honest limits: TurboMind’s CUDA path is NVIDIA-centric, so AMD and other accelerators effectively route you to the PyTorch engine, which trades some peak throughput for portability. The quantization toolkit covers weight-only flows well, but the calibration stage wants a representative dataset to produce good scales, and the resulting checkpoints are engine-specific artifacts. Finally, the codebase moves fast — model support and kernel paths shift between releases, so pin a version in production and expect to re-verify flags when you upgrade. None of that dims the core appeal: two complete engines, one clean interface, and a codebase that teaches serving systems in two languages at once.
entry.summary: How lmdeploy pairs a pure-PyTorch engine with a hand-tuned C++ and CUDA TurboMind core behind a single OpenAI-compatible serving layer.

entry.title: One Model, Every Device - Inside mlc-ai/mlc-llm

link.title: One Model, Every Device - Inside mlc-ai/mlc-llm

entry.content:
Most inference frameworks ask you to meet the model on the model’s terms: a datacenter GPU, a CUDA driver, a Python runtime, and a lot of VRAM. mlc-llm from the mlc-ai team flips that arrangement. It treats a large language model as a program to be compiled, then emits a tailored artifact for whichever machine you actually own — a laptop with an Apple GPU, an Android phone with an Adreno chip, or even a browser tab running on WebGPU.

The repository, licensed under Apache-2.0, is organized around that compiler mindset. Python source under python/mlc_llm defines architectures and a long sequence of graph rewrites, while a compact C++ core under cpp/serve executes the compiled result with a real batch scheduler, samplers, and speculative decoding. A FastAPI layer on top speaks the OpenAI chat-completions dialect, so anything that already talks to a hosted model can be pointed at a locally compiled one with a single URL change. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The overview traces the two halves of the project: a compile-time path that turns model definitions into optimized artifacts, and a runtime path that serves them from server down to phone.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The compile command is the front door for the compiler: given a model and a target GPU, it drives the entire lowering sequence and writes out a loadable model library.
  • Inside the compiler passes directory, graph rewrites fuse weight dequantization into matrix multiplies, pick KV cache strategies, and specialize kernels for small batches.
  • The dequantization fusion pass is a representative example of why compilation matters: decompressing weights right before they are consumed avoids extra memory round-trips.
  • Quantization schemes live under quantization, where group-wise scales squeeze a 16-bit checkpoint into 4-bit storage with controllable accuracy trade-offs.
  • The model preset table is the single largest Python file in the repo, encoding per-model context lengths, vocab sizes, and defaults for dozens of architectures.
  • At runtime, the MLC engine batches concurrent requests, streams tokens asynchronously, and exposes OpenAI-style chat and completion objects straight from Python.
  • The wire surface is defined by protocol models, so the same engine backs the REST server and the in-process API without duplicated logic.
  • Beneath Python, the C++ serving core runs the actual batch loop, and the same native core is what gets packaged into the Android runtime for phones.

Why You Need This

If you have ever tried to hand a 7-billion-parameter model to a machine without a datacenter GPU, the usual answer is “buy hardware.” mlc-llm takes a different route: it rewrites the model itself for the hardware you have. The group quantization module stores weights in compact blocks with per-group scales, and because the compiler knows about this layout, the generated kernels dequantize on the fly inside the matmul itself. The result is that a 4-bit Llama variant fits in a few gigabytes and still runs at interactive speed, because bandwidth, not FLOPs, is the real ceiling on consumer machines.

The second reason is operational. Because the engine speaks the standard chat-completions shape through protocol definitions, existing client code — LangChain loops, IDE extensions, home-automation scripts — keeps working unchanged when you swap the base URL from a hosted provider to http://127.0.0.1:8000. The MLC engine additionally supports structured output through grammar-constrained decoding, which matters if you need the model to emit valid JSON for a downstream parser rather than plausible-looking prose.

The third reason is the platform story, which is genuinely unusual among open-source inference stacks. The native batch scheduler in C++ engine core is the same code that ships inside the Android app, meaning the prefix caching, continuous batching, and speculative decoding you get on a server are not server-only luxuries. A conversation started in the radix tree KV cache on a laptop and the same mechanism on a phone share one implementation lineage, which dramatically cuts the cost of supporting three or four platforms at once.

The detail graph follows one compile-and-serve journey: CLI subcommands feed the pass sequence, the model zoo supplies architectures and weights, the Python engine orchestrates requests, and the native core executes them on each platform.

Start in the CLI layer at the top left. Each subcommand in python/mlc_llm/interface is thin: chat.py wires a terminal loop to the engine, serve.py mounts the FastAPI routes, gen_config.py derives a conversation template from a Hugging Face checkpoint, and convert_weight.py rewrites a checkpoint into a chosen quantization scheme before anything is compiled. The JIT wrapper in interface/jit.py deserves a mention: when a user requests a model that has no cached artifact, it triggers compilation on the fly and caches the result, which is how the popular prebuilt endpoints on the Hugging Face hub stay reproducible.

Follow the arrows down into the compilation stack and the model zoo. The ordered pass flow file inside compiler_pass sequences rewrites that would otherwise be hand-written kernel work: fusing dequantization into matmuls, dispatching the right KV cache creation per architecture, estimating peak memory so the runtime can size its pools, and rewriting the graph for tensor parallelism across multiple GPUs. The model zoo side is equally concrete — model/model.py registers each architecture by name, presets fill in per-model constants, and the Hugging Face loader in loader/huggingface_loader.py streams safetensors shards with lazy mapping so a 30-billion-parameter checkpoint does not need 30 gigabytes of RAM to open.

The serving half on the right is where requests live. The async engine in serve/engine.py subclasses a shared base that handles tokenization, stop conditions, and state tracking; each incoming completion request becomes an entry in a batch that the native core steps forward. Inside cpp/serve, the engine action files show the design clearly: engine_actions/batch_prefill_base.cc chunks prompt processing, engine_actions/eagle_batch_verify.cc verifies speculative draft tokens in one shot, and sampler/gpu_sampler.cc applies temperature and top-p on-device. The two radix trees — Python and C++ — mirror each other so prefix reuse works regardless of which layer drives the cache.

From Install to a Running Chat

The quickest path skips compilation entirely because the team publishes prebuilt quantized artifacts on the Hugging Face hub. Install the wheel into a conda environment, then run mlc_llm chat HF://mlc-ai/Llama-3-8B-Instruct-q4f16_1-MLC for an interactive terminal session, or mlc_llm serve HF://mlc-ai/Llama-3-8B-Instruct-q4f16_1-MLC to bring up a REST server on port 8000 that any OpenAI-compatible client can call. In Python, from mlc_llm import MLCEngine gives you an engine whose .chat.completions.create accepts the same message format you already use against hosted APIs, with streaming supported out of the box. If your GPU is unusual or you want a different quantization, mlc_llm compile builds a fresh library from a local checkpoint, and the same command path powers the mobile packaging for Android and iOS builds.

Honest limits: compilation is where the complexity bill arrives. Building a model library for a new target requires a working TVM toolchain and the right Vulkan, Metal, CUDA, or ROCm backend installed, and first-time builds are neither quick nor silent — expect compiler logs and disk usage. The engine targets text generation; multimodal support exists for selected vision-language models but is not the default path, and some newer architectures land in the model zoo with a lag while presets and templates are added. Finally, while the C++ core is compact and readable, the compilation passes assume TVM fluency — if a generated kernel misbehaves, debugging means reading graph rewrites rather than plain PyTorch code. For teams that want one model artifact to span server, laptop, phone, and browser, though, that trade is the entire point of the project.
entry.summary: How mlc-llm uses machine learning compilation to turn Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek checkpoints into optimized artifacts that run on GPUs, phones, and browsers.

entry.title: The Server That Powered Hugging Chat - Inside huggingface/text-generation-inference

link.title: The Server That Powered Hugging Chat - Inside huggingface/text-generation-inference

entry.content:
Before every lab had its own serving stack, Hugging Face had to solve the problem for the whole ecosystem. Text Generation Inference, Apache-2.0-licensed and written in Rust with a Python GPU core, is the toolkit that powered Hugging Chat, the Inference API, and Inference Endpoints for years of production traffic. The README describes it plainly: a Rust, Python and gRPC server for text generation inference, with tensor parallelism for multi-GPU models, continuous batching of incoming requests, token streaming over Server-Sent Events, a Messages API compatible with OpenAI Chat Completion, and quantization ranging from bitsandbytes and GPT-Q through EETQ, AWQ, Marlin, and fp8. Speculative decoding with Medusa heads promises roughly doubled latency, watermarking implements the Sotoudeh-Gerard green-list scheme, and safetensors weight loading keeps the security story clean by never executing pickled checkpoints.

The layout tells you immediately that this is a distributed system, not a library. The launcher directory holds a Rust supervisor that downloads weights, assigns GPUs, and spawns everything else; the router directory holds the Axum HTTP server that validates requests and builds batches; the server directory holds one Python gRPC service per GPU; and the backends directory carries alternative engines like llama.cpp and TensorRT-LLM that speak the same contract. Between them sits proto/generate.proto, the protobuf definition that decouples web concerns from GPU work so completely that either side can be replaced independently. Reading it is a masterclass in how to slice a latency-sensitive system along process boundaries. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

TGI at a glance: the Rust launcher spawns the router and one Python shard per GPU, requests flow through validation and the continuous batcher, cross the gRPC contract into the shard's flash causal LM, which allocates paged KV cache slots and dispatches to attention kernels, while alternative backends can serve the same wire protocol.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts in the launcher at launcher/src/main.rs, which parses flags, downloads model files, and supervises child processes.
  • HTTP traffic lands in the Axum server at router/src/server.rs, which mounts generate, stream, chat, and health routes with tracing and metrics middleware.
  • OpenAI-style conversations are handled by the chat module at router/src/chat.rs, which applies the model’s chat template and parses tool calls back out of the stream.
  • Every request passes through the validator at router/src/validation.rs, which clamps token budgets and rejects malformed sampling parameters before they can poison a batch.
  • Validated requests join the batcher at router/src/infer/mod.rs, the continuous batching queue that coalesces work and fans token streams back to clients.
  • The wire format lives in proto/generate.proto, defining the Shard service with its prefill, decode, and health RPCs.
  • On the other side sits the Python shard at server/text_generation_server/server.py, which warms up the model on boot and serves the generation loop.
  • The core wrapper is the flash causal LM at server/text_generation_server/models/flash_causal_lm.py, where paged cache slots and batched forward passes meet.

Why You Need This

The first reason is that this codebase is a complete blueprint for request admission control. The validator at router/src/validation.rs is a single shared object that knows the model’s max sequence length, maximum batch total tokens, and stop-sequence rules, so every route gets identical guardrails for free. Once past the gate, requests enter the batcher at router/src/infer/mod.rs, which pairs each caller with a oneshot channel, applies queue timeouts, and decides when the next continuous batch should form. This is the exact machinery that keeps a saturated server responsive: new work slips into the current decode step without waiting for earlier requests to finish, and slow consumers are dropped rather than allowed to stall the fleet.

The second reason is the GPU layering, which reads like a textbook on inference arithmetic. Quantized linear algebra lives in dedicated modules such as the fp8 layer at server/text_generation_server/layers/fp8.py and the Marlin kernels used for 4-bit weights, while the tensor parallel primitives at server/text_generation_server/layers/tensor_parallel.py wrap all-reduce and all-gather so a single Linear layer can span eight GPUs. LoRA serving is handled by the adapter layer at server/text_generation_server/layers/lora.py, which applies batched low-rank updates on top of frozen base weights, and speculative decoding rides the Medusa heads at server/text_generation_server/layers/medusa.py, which propose several future tokens per step for the target model to verify. Each concern is isolated, testable, and composable.

The third reason is the pluggable backend architecture, which solves a problem every inference provider eventually faces: supporting engines that are not your code. The launcher can hand serving to the llama.cpp backend implemented at backends/llamacpp/src/backend.rs or the TensorRT-LLM backend at backends/trtllm/src/lib.rs, and both speak the identical protobuf contract defined in generate.proto. The router does not know or care that the GPU side changed. For anyone building a model-routing service, this is the cleanest working example of how to standardize an inference wire protocol without sacrificing per-engine optimization, and it explains why so many later serving stacks converged on similar designs.

The detailed view follows one request from CLI flags through the launcher, router internals, protobuf wire, and into the Python model zoo, where causal, seq2seq, Mamba, and vision-language wrappers share one generation skeleton over quantized GPU layers.

The detail walk starts on the Rust side, where the launcher’s argument parser doubles as the product surface: memory fraction, quantization mode, max batch tokens, and watermark flags all become environment variables and process spawns. The router internals show that chat templating is a first-class subsystem, with the template engine at router/src/infer/chat_template.rs rendering Jinja with tool schemas, and the grammar builder at router/src/infer/tool_grammar.rs compiling function definitions into constrained grammars so the model can only emit valid JSON arguments. Crossing the wire, the Python side opens with a zoo of model wrappers: the base abstraction at server/text_generation_server/models/model.py defines the generate_token contract, and specialized children cover encoder-decoder families in server/text_generation_server/models/seq2seq_lm.py as well as the state-space Mamba wrapper at server/text_generation_server/models/mamba.py, which generates by passing compressed state instead of attention keys.

The bottom half of the detail diagram is where the performance lives. The weights reader at server/text_generation_server/utils/weights.py memory-maps sharded safetensors files, resolves which shard holds a tensor by suffix rules, and feeds quantization-aware layers directly, so eight GPUs can load one model without ever materializing the full checkpoint in RAM. Sampling is a stack of composable processors in server/text_generation_server/utils/logits_process.py, implementing temperature, top-k, top-p, and typical-p, with the watermark processor at server/text_generation_server/utils/watermark.py slotting in as one more bias before the final softmax. This is the part of the codebase worth reading with a notebook open.

From Install to First Token

The fastest path is the official container: run docker with the ghcr.io/huggingface/text-generation-inference:3.3.5 image, pass a volume for the weight cache and a model id like HuggingFaceH4/zephyr-7b-beta, and the launcher handles download, sharding, and boot. Within a minute or two, port 8080 speaks both TGI’s native /generate_stream route and the OpenAI-compatible /v1/chat/completions route, so you can point any existing client library at it and get streaming tokens back over Server-Sent Events. The Python client package in clients/python offers a typed alternative for scripts, and the README documents quantization flags you can add to the same command line to fit bigger models onto smaller cards.

Honest limits: the README itself opens with a caution that text-generation-inference is now in maintenance mode, accepting only minor fixes while the team recommends downstream engines such as vLLM and SGLang that build on transformers architectures directly. That makes this repository less a tool to bet your roadmap on and more a reference implementation to study: the process boundaries, the batching discipline, and the quantization layering are all patterns that survived into the engines that superseded it. The hardware support table also reads NVIDIA, AMD, Inferentia, Intel GPU, Gaudi, and TPU, but the depth of optimization varies by platform, and the newest model architectures will land in the actively maintained forks first. Read it like a well-commented textbook that the authors have archived, not a car you should still drive daily.
entry.summary: A source-code tour of Text Generation Inference, the Rust and Python serving stack behind Hugging Chat: the launcher that shards GPUs, the Axum router with continuous batching, the gRPC contract that separates web from GPU work, paged KV cache slots, quantized layers, and pluggable backends like llama.cpp and TensorRT-LLM.

entry.title: Google ADK: Workflow Agents That Never Call the Model - Inside google/adk-python

link.title: Google ADK: Workflow Agents That Never Call the Model - Inside google/adk-python

entry.content:
Every agent framework eventually confronts the same problem: when you wire five agents together, the wiring itself becomes code that a language model can get wrong. Google’s Agent Development Kit answers with a pattern no other major framework ships as a first-class citizen — workflow agents that compose sub-agents with zero model calls. A SequentialAgent runs its children in order. A ParallelAgent fans out and merges their event streams. A LoopAgent iterates until an escalation event or a max iteration count, with a purpose-built exit tool the inner agent can call. The model never sees the control flow, because the control flow is Python. That idea anchors an Apache-2.0 codebase of unusual industrial polish: a runner that streams every intermediate event, a flow built from composable request processors, toolsets that filter themselves per request, a plugin system hooked into every lifecycle stage, and a fleet of swappable services for sessions, memory, artifacts, and authentication. It is the framework Google ships Gemini in, and reading it explains a lot about how Google thinks agents should be built.

The architecture reads as five strata. At the top, the Runner turns a new or resumed invocation into an event stream, coordinating session, artifact, and memory services as it goes. Agents form a small hierarchy — a base class owning the lifecycle, LlmAgent as the model-driven workhorse, and the workflow agents as deterministic composers — and every agent’s behavior flows through a processor chain in the flows package, where separate processors assemble identity, instructions, and contents, build tool declarations, and execute function calls. The model layer hides Gemini behind an interface that a registry resolves, with a three-thousand-seven-hundred-line LiteLLM bridge and a native Anthropic client standing in for the rest of the market. Services — sessions with state deltas, keyword-searched memory, versioned artifacts, OAuth credential exchange — arrive as interfaces with in-memory, SQLite, database, and Vertex implementations. And the edges are real product surfaces: a CLI that runs agents in the terminal, a FastAPI server behind adk web and adk api_server, an evaluation harness that scores trajectories from case files. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

ADK at a glance: the runner drives the agent hierarchy and its workflow composers, every LLM agent runs through the processor-chain flow, toolsets and the model registry arm it, plugins hook the lifecycle, and session services plus the API server turn it into a deployed product.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The runner turns invocations into event streams and coordinates every state service.
  • The agent base owns the lifecycle every agent shares, callbacks included.
  • The LLM agent is the model-driven workhorse with instructions, tools and output schemas.
  • The workflow agents compose sub-agents deterministically as Sequential, Parallel and Loop.
  • The base flow runs the request processors, the model call, then the response processors.
  • The toolset contract groups tools with per-request filtering and auth wiring.
  • The LiteLLM bridge adapts a hundred providers onto the model interface.
  • The API server exposes runs, sessions and live audio over FastAPI.

Why You Need This

The first reason is the workflow agents, because they settle the framework argument about orchestration by refusing to let the model do it. The base class defines one async lifecycle — runAsync with an invocation context — that all agents share, so a ParallelAgent’s children are indistinguishable from a solo LlmAgent to whoever runs them. SequentialAgent is under two hundred lines because composition is genuinely that thin: it iterates children, threading session state between them. ParallelAgent merges child event branches so concurrent sub-agents stay attributable, and LoopAgent iterates until an escalation or cap, with the exit tool as the model’s one deliberate way out. The transfer between model-driven and deterministic layers is itself an interface: the transfer tool and the flow’s transfer processor let an LlmAgent hand control to a sibling, so you can mix “model decides” and “code decides” per subtree. For anyone who has debugged an agent that wander-routed through its own menu, this design is the alternative worth copying.

The second reason is the processor chain, because it decomposes the black box of “what does the model actually see.” The base flow runs a list of request processors before each model call and response processors after, and each processor is a readable module: the basic processors inject identity and static instructions, the functions processor builds tool declarations and executes requested calls, and the transfer processor appends routing instructions. The machinery underneath is honest about the hard parts — declaration building from type hints, argument coercion of model-produced JSON, the ToolContext that gives every tool a handle on state, artifacts, memory, and auth. Events carry the side effects: EventActions bundle state deltas, artifact saves, transfers, and escalations, which is how the runner replays and rewinds sessions deterministically. The plugin system wraps all of it — base_plugin.py exposes callbacks from user input through model calls to tool errors, and the shipped plugins from debug logging to reflect-and-retry are worked examples.

The third reason is the services layer, because deployment is where most agent demos die, and ADK treats it as a first-class surface. The session services come in four grades — in-memory for tests, SQLite and full database for production, Vertex-backed for Google Cloud — all exposing the same state-delta model the events produce. Memory is a searchable bank the agent queries mid-run, and artifacts are versioned binaries in memory, on disk, or in GCS. The auth handler performs OAuth exchanges on tool calls with resume support, so a tool that needs a login token suspends and continues instead of failing. On the model side, the registry resolves names to implementations, the Gemini client ships with a context-cache manager for cost control, a fallback model wraps primaries with ordered backups, and the interface contract is small enough that the bridge is integration, not surgery.

The detail view: the runner with its contexts, events and compaction; the flow processors from identity to function calling; tool internals from declarations to the transfer verb; model implementations from Gemini through LiteLLM with fallback and caching; the state services with auth; and the CLI, server, evaluation and agent-to-agent surfaces.

The detail view shows the seams explicitly. The runner threads an invocation context through everything, streams events, and compacts long sessions — while the flow remains a pure function of that context. Tool internals sit one layer below the processor so the model-facing contract (declarations, parsing, confirmation) is separable from the agent-facing verbs (transfer, exit, memory load). The model group is deliberately boring — interface, three implementations, resilience, caching — because the interesting decisions live in the services and the processor chain. The interface stratum on the right is what makes this a product rather than a library: the CLI drives dev loops, the test runner scores evaluation cases against real trajectories, and the remote A2A agent — two thousand lines, marked experimental — wraps external agents speaking the agent-to-agent protocol into the same lifecycle as local ones.

From Install to a Multi-Agent Tree

Installation is pip install google-adk, and the fastest path is a folder with one agent: define an Agent named root with instructions and a tool or two, run adk web in the parent directory, and the dev UI serves the agent at localhost with tracing visible per turn. To feel the workflow-agent idea, split the work — a SequentialAgent whose children are a researcher LlmAgent, a ParallelAgent fanning out three summarizers, and a LoopAgent with a reviewer that escalates when done — then compose them as sub_agents. Run the same tree headlessly with adk api_server for HTTP clients, or adk run root for the terminal. Swap InMemorySessionService for DatabaseSessionService with a connection URL and the conversation state survives restarts; add adk eval with a case file and the trajectories are scored automatically. The evaluation CLI and the deployment helpers (adk deploy) are the bridge from notebook to service, and both read the same agent folder structure you already have.

Honest limits: the docs and defaults are Gemini-first, and the deepest integrations — Vertex session and memory backends, context caching, grounding tools — assume Google Cloud, so a non-GCP deployment is supported but noticeably less paved. The evaluation harness expects its own case-file format, which is an investment in lock-in however well-designed. The agent-to-agent surface is explicitly experimental and its two-thousand-line wrapper is best treated as a preview. And the framework’s breadth is a real cost: the plugin, toolset, and service abstractions are all load-bearing, so new teams should start with the workflow agents and plain function tools before reaching for the customization points that make ADK powerful.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of google/adk-python: the Agent Development Kit where Sequential, Parallel and Loop agents compose sub-agents deterministically, a processor-chain flow assembles every model request, toolsets and plugins extend the runtime, and sessions, memory, artifacts and auth arrive as swappable services.

entry.title: Claude Code: The Open Surface of a Closed Binary - Inside anthropics/claude-code

link.title: Claude Code: The Open Surface of a Closed Binary - Inside anthropics/claude-code

entry.content:
Claude Code is the most-discussed terminal agent in software, and almost none of its code is public. The binary you install is proprietary, licensed under commercial terms, and built somewhere you cannot read. So why does the repository deserve a source tour? Because this is not a mirror of the product — it is the product’s open surface, and it is more instructive than most projects’ full source. Four mods that ship compiled into the binary publish their complete TypeScript here. Thirteen official plugins demonstrate the entire extension format in markdown and Python. The infrastructure automation that runs Claude against the project’s own issues sits in the same tree, next to a checker that fails the build the moment any workflow breaks the security rules for calling Claude. If you want to know how the most commercially successful coding agent expects to be extended, hardened, and operated, this repository is the specification, written in working code.

The architecture reads as three rings around a hidden center. The center is the engine itself, present only as a name in README files and as type declarations. The inner ring is the mods — four TypeScript hook modules under mods/ whose README explains a genuinely novel design: each one is a register(on, options) entry that hooks engine events with middleware-style functions, and they coordinate through typed “noun contracts” rather than direct calls. The middle ring is the plugins — self-contained folders of slash commands, subagents, skills, and hooks, from a five-agent review crew to a plugin that watches your conversations and writes enforcement hooks for behaviors it catches you repeating. The outer ring is operations: GitHub workflows that triage issues with the agent itself, a hardening job that polices those workflows, and gateway examples that put corporate cloud endpoints in front of the binary. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Claude Code at a glance: the closed engine exposes its contracts and marketplace, four built-in mods seat themselves around it, official plugins demonstrate the extension format, repository automation runs the agent on its own issues under a hardening checker, and gateway examples route enterprise traffic.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The install story documents the proprietary binary this repository surrounds.
  • The typed extension surface is the declaration file mods import against, including the testing kit.
  • The plugin catalog lists every official plugin the install command can fetch.
  • The security seat keeps an organization’s managed policy out of reach of installed plugins.
  • The diff pane module renders uncommitted changes beside the transcript as edits happen.
  • The instruction loader gives AGENTS.md files the same treatment the engine gives CLAUDE.md.
  • The rule engine matches enforcement rules against tool calls for the hookify plugin.
  • The hardening checker fails CI when a workflow calls Claude without the required protections.

Why You Need This

The first reason is the mods, because they are the deepest public look at how a closed product structures its own extension points. The mods README defines the pattern: a mod is a plugin whose behavior lives in one register(on, options) function, where on subscribes to engine events and each handler is a ($, e, next) function — middleware, with next continuing down the chain. The diff module uses it to keep a pane of uncommitted changes current, probing the terminal first through its backend detection. The composition rule is the elegant part: the telemetry module owns the $.telemetry noun and keeps its types in one declaration file, and any mod that records events imports that contract rather than copying it — the typechecker rejects an implementation that drifts from what callers read. The security seat sits outermost on managed machines, and its verdict ranking decides how permission decisions from users and policy tiers outrank each other. Add the testing kit — mock.clock, mock.env, a tier('builtin') harness that answers engine calls from memory — and you have a complete essay on plugin architecture published as a side effect of shipping a binary.

The second reason is the plugin format, because the thirteen folders under plugins/ are the reference implementations Anthropic ships for it. The structure is deliberately boring — a manifest, a hooks manifest, and directories of markdown — and the structure skill teaches it in three hundred seventy lines. The interesting part is what the format can express. hookify is a self-writing enforcement system: a conversation analyzer reads your transcripts for repeated unwanted behavior, the rule engine turns the findings into matchable rules, and a PreToolUse hook intercepts every tool call to apply them. The review command runs five parallel reviewer agents and filters their findings through confidence scoring to suppress false positives. ralph-wiggum loops the same task until completion, with a Stop hook that refuses to let the session end. And security-guidance matches edited code against nine pattern classes — command injection, eval, unsafe deserialization — to warn before risky changes land.

The third reason is the automation, because this repository is a worked example of an agent maintaining its own project under guardrails. The triage workflow labels and routes new issues, claude.yml answers @claude mentions, and a maintenance script handles duplicate reports and lifecycle comments. None of that runs on trust: the hardening workflow invokes three hundred five lines of Python that verify every Claude-calling job runs on an egress-firewall runner, keeps a network allow list in enforce mode, and requires explicit permission modes on every step — with an exemption table for the jobs that cannot comply and a rule that the build fails when protections are weakened. The repository even documents its own rules in a CLAUDE.md written for coding agents, and ships gateway examples showing how enterprises route the binary through AWS Bedrock or GCP Vertex instead of the public endpoint.

The detail view: the engine hub and its contracts on the left, the four built-in mods with their internals, the official plugins from hookify to security guidance, the GitHub automation layer with its hardening checker, and the cloud gateway examples on the right.

The detail view shows how the rings interlock. Every mod edge runs through the declaration file — the diff register probes backend renderers, the agents-md register walks for unseen instruction files, the security seat ranks verdicts and gates admission — so the types are the coordination point, not a shared runtime. On the plugin side, the flows are end-to-end: the hookify command spawns its analyzer, the analyzer feeds the rule engine, the engine is enforced by the PreToolUse process; the security reminder hook matches patterns on every file edit. The automation layer closes on itself — the hardening checker audits both Claude workflows, the triage workflow delegates to the sweep script — which is the picture of a project that lets the agent act but keeps the enforcement in code humans review. The GCP counterpart completes the deployment story with Vertex routing and its own Terraform.

From Install to a Hardened Session

Installation is one line — curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash on macOS or Linux, irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex on Windows, or a Homebrew cask and a winget package — after which running claude in any project directory starts the session. To see the extension system from the receiving end, run /plugin and install from the marketplace catalog, or read a built-in mod running from source with claude --plugin-dir mods/diff — the README’s own suggestion. If you want to build rather than observe, the plugin-dev plugin is a bootstrapping kit: its create-plugin command walks eight phases with validator agents, and its seven skills cover commands, subagents, hooks, skills, MCP integration, and settings. For contributors to this repository specifically, tsc -p mods/tsconfig.json typechecks every mod against the contracts, and claude plugin test mods/diff runs a mod’s tests against a mock engine — the same gates the repository’s own CI applies before anything merges.

Honest limits: the engine is not here, so no amount of reading explains the model-facing internals — context management, tool scheduling, the terminal UI all stay opaque. The license is Anthropic’s commercial terms, not an open-source license, so the code you can read is reference material rather than something you can fork into a product. The hooks-module API the mods use is marked early access and may change between releases without notice, and the mods are deliberately excluded from the marketplace listing since the copies that matter ship in the binary. Finally, the plugins are examples by the project’s own description — good ones, but examples — so production teams should treat them as starting points and review the hooks before installing them anywhere that matters.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of anthropics/claude-code: the repository behind the closed-source terminal agent, where four built-in mods ship their TypeScript hook modules in the open, thirteen official plugins demonstrate the extension format, and GitHub Actions run Claude on the project's own issues under a hardening checker that fails the build when its rules are broken.

entry.title: The Node Graph That Runs Any Diffusion Model - Inside comfyanonymous/ComfyUI

link.title: The Node Graph That Runs Any Diffusion Model - Inside comfyanonymous/ComfyUI

entry.content:
If you have generated an AI image in the last two years, odds are ComfyUI touched it. ComfyUI is the GPL-3.0 node-graph engine that has become the de facto way to run diffusion models locally: you wire boxes like Load Checkpoint, KSampler, and VAE Decode into a canvas, hit queue, and the engine figures out memory, ordering, and execution. The README makes bold but defensible claims — the most optimized diffusion inference engine for local consumer hardware, big models running on as little as 4GB of VRAM plus 8GB of RAM via asynchronous weight streaming — and backs them with native support for an enormous model catalog: SD1.5 through SD3.5, Flux, Qwen Image, Wan 2.2, HunyuanVideo, audio models like ACE-Step, 3D generators, and more. Weekly releases chase the model wave, a template library keeps the workflows current, and workflows save as JSON you can version control, with seeds recoverable from the media they produced.

Under the hood it is a masterclass in systems engineering: an aiohttp server that streams execution events over websocket, a cache-aware graph executor that re-runs only what changed, a node registry with hundreds of modules, and a model management layer that treats VRAM as a budgeted resource rather than a prayer. For anyone building AI tooling, the repository doubles as free education. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

ComfyUI at a glance: a server serving the node editor on top, a validated and cache-aware executor in the middle, a growing node registry, and the VRAM-managed diffusion core underneath.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The launcher — parses CLI arguments, imports the whole node registry, and boots the server with async-friendly settings.
  • The HTTP server — the aiohttp app holding routes for prompts, history, and model lists, plus the websocket that streams live execution events to the editor.
  • The folder path registry — maps each model type to directories on disk, extended by extra_model_paths.yaml for external drives and NAS mounts.
  • The graph executor — validates, walks, and runs the workflow node by node with interruption and error surfacing.
  • The cache strategy — hashes node inputs so unchanged branches of a re-queued workflow skip instantly.
  • The core nodes — KSampler, checkpoint and LoRA loaders, VAE encode and decode, conditioning, and image IO for the classic loop.
  • The model manager — the VRAM ledger that loads, offloads, and asynchronously streams weights per GPU.
  • The samplers — the denoising loop with CFG, noise, and dozens of named algorithms from Euler to DPM++.

Why You Need This

The first reason is brute practicality: ComfyUI runs models other tools cannot, and keeps running them when VRAM runs out. The magic lives in the model manager, which maintains a live accounting of every GPU’s VRAM, decides when to load and offload, and streams weights asynchronously so the compute stays saturated even when the model exceeds memory. Detection is clever too: the model detector recognizes architectures by prefix-matching weight names against the model registry, which is how a single install keeps absorbing every new checkpoint format the community invents without breaking old ones. Quantized formats ride the same path through the quantized operation classes, so low-bit checkpoints are first-class citizens rather than hacks.

The second reason is the execution model, which is worth stealing ideas from. When you re-queue an edited workflow, the graph executor walks only what changed: the cache strategy fingerprints each node’s inputs and reuses outputs for identical subgraphs, so tweaking a prompt at the end of a fifty-node graph does not re-run the fifty nodes before it. Validation happens before execution — type checks, file existence, even dry runs — progress streams over websocket, and jobs can be interrupted cleanly mid-node. If you have ever built a task engine, the package under comfy_execution is a compact reference implementation of partial re-execution, with the job state machine in jobs.py making long-running graphs observable instead of opaque.

The third reason is the extensibility contract. Everything users see is a node, and nodes are plain Python classes registered in mappings: the core nodes cover the classic text-to-image loop, while the extras catalog adds everything newer — video models, audio, 3D, upscalers, masks — and paid partner nodes plug in closed models behind the same interface. Modifiers compose elegantly too: the model patcher applies LoRA and hooks as copy-on-write patches so multiple workflows can share one set of loaded weights without corrupting each other, and the samplers sit beneath it all as a clean library of denoising math.

The detail view: server and execution machinery at the top, the node registries in the middle, and the model layer, conditioning stack, and sampling loop that actually produce pixels below.

The detail diagram rewards a slow read, because the model layer is where ComfyUI earns its reputation. A checkpoint arrives through the loader in comfy/sd.py, gets identified by the detector, and materializes as a BaseModel with its own sampling schedule and latent format. Around it, the patcher wraps the weights with copy-on-write semantics, LoRA and hooks contribute their patches, and patched operation classes replace plain torch calls so every forward pass honors them. This is why a dozen workflows can share one loaded checkpoint while each applies different LoRAs: the shared weights are never mutated, only viewed through per-workflow patch sets. Meanwhile the model manager watches the VRAM ledger, using the memory utilities to survive out-of-memory conditions by soft-emptying caches instead of crashing — the difference between a failed queue item and a lost afternoon.

On the conditioning side, the CLIP encoder stack handles the multi-tokenizer reality of modern models — CLIP plus T5, or LLaMA variants — while ControlNet injects spatial guidance during sampling. The sampling group ties it together: helpers prepare conditioning and ControlNet, context windows chunk long generations for video models, and the sampler loop consumes sigmas from the sampling schedule, feeding latents that the VAE finally turns into pixels. Notably, the paid partner nodes register into the same mapping as everything else, and an –offline flag keeps the core from touching the network unless you ask — a refreshing stance for a project with its own hosted cloud offering.

From Install to a First Image

The zero-effort path is the desktop application for Windows and macOS from comfy.org/download, which bundles Python and the frontend. From source on any OS, clone the repository, pip install -r requirements.txt, drop Stable Diffusion or Flux checkpoints into the models/checkpoints directory, and run python main.py; the UI opens at http://127.0.0.1:8188. Then either drag a template from the workflow library onto the canvas or build the minimal Load Checkpoint, CLIP Text Encode, Empty Latent Image, KSampler, VAE Decode, Save Image chain by hand — queue it and watch the websocket stream each node’s progress live. AMD, Intel, Apple Silicon, and Ascend GPUs are all supported per the README, extra model locations can be wired in with the provided YAML example, and subgraphs let you package a working cluster of nodes into one reusable box once your workflow grows.

Honest limits: the node canvas has a learning curve that templates only soften, and reading someone else’s dense graph can feel like archaeology; the model zoo moves weekly, so expect updates to be frequent and occasionally disruptive; the paid API nodes require accounts and keys, though –offline keeps everything local; and the GPL-3.0 license matters if you embed ComfyUI in products. None of that offsets the value: whether you generate images or not, reading how this codebase budgets VRAM, caches graphs, and patches models is a free education in practical ML systems engineering.
entry.summary: A guided tour of the ComfyUI source tree: the aiohttp server, cache-aware graph execution, the node registry, VRAM-aware model management, model patching, and the sampler math underneath.

entry.title: Turn Your Desk Into an AI Cluster - Inside exo-explore/exo

link.title: Turn Your Desk Into an AI Cluster - Inside exo-explore/exo

entry.content:
Every Mac on your desk is a supercomputer that spends most of its life idle. exo-explore/exo is the open-source project that bands those machines together into one logical AI cluster, so a model too large for any single device can run comfortably across all of them. It discovers peers with zero configuration, elects a coordinator, weighs each device’s memory and each link’s bandwidth, and then shards the model with tensor parallelism. The README reports up to 1.8x speedup on two devices and 3.2x on four, with day-0 RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 cutting inter-device latency by 99 percent. The project is Apache-2.0 licensed and maintained by exo labs, with a dashboard at localhost:52415 for watching the cluster breathe. The README’s own screenshots show four 512GB M3 Ultra Mac Studios jointly serving DeepSeek v3.1 and Kimi K2 Thinking, which is the kind of demonstration that used to require a rack in a datacenter.

What makes the codebase worth a tour is that it is a complete distributed systems education in miniature: a Rust discovery layer, an election protocol, a placement solver, a supervision tree, and four API dialects, all in a few thousand readable lines. The tree is pleasantly polyglot — Python for every process under src/exo, Rust under rust/networking for peer discovery and transport, a Swift macOS app under app, and a Node dashboard under dashboard — yet each part speaks to the others through one small event vocabulary. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The exo architecture at a glance: one API surface and dashboard on top, a discovery-and-election fabric underneath, an elected master computing placements, and workers executing tensor-parallel inference.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A single command boots the world — the CLI entry starts the API, dashboard, and either master or worker roles on each machine.
  • Rust multicast discovery — a UDP beacon shouts hello on the LAN so devices find each other with no manual configuration.
  • The live topology graph — nodes and weighted links, updated in realtime as devices join, sleep, or move between networks.
  • Master election — a heartbeat protocol with seniority and retry backoff picks one coordinator and survives its crash.
  • The master controller — consumes events from the bus, updates cluster state, and issues commands back onto it.
  • The placement engine — fits model shards onto devices using memory limits and link quality, choosing the best device cycles.
  • The tensor parallel engine — rewrites MLX layers into distributed shards so big models run across small machines.
  • The API server — one FastAPI app on port 52415 that accepts OpenAI, Claude, and Ollama requests and streams tokens back.

Why You Need This

The first reason is raw capability. A 671B-parameter model in 8-bit needs roughly 700 GB of unified memory, which no laptop holds, yet four Mac Studios hold it easily. The machinery that makes this real is the placement engine working with the tensor parallel engine: the master computes which shard lands on which device, and the worker rewrites each attention and MLP layer into a distributed version whose partial results are summed across the ring. Because exo accounts for link bandwidth when choosing device cycles, adding a faster path such as Thunderbolt 5 actually makes the cluster faster rather than merely bigger. That is the difference between a science project and a tool: the benchmark images in the repository were produced by an independent blogger who wired four machines over Thunderbolt and published the tokens-per-second numbers, which is exactly the kind of reproducibility open source should enable.

The second reason is that it feels like magic but is honestly engineered. You install nothing on the network, run nothing as administrator, and yet machines find each other. That is the Rust discovery module, which multicasts hello beacons and answers them, plus master election, which resolves the inevitable question of who is in charge. When a master goes silent for thirty seconds, a follower runs a new election with growing backoff, and the cluster reorganizes itself without a restart. Reading these two files teaches more about practical consensus and discovery than most tutorials. There are even practical touches for shared spaces: the EXO_ZENOH_NAMESPACE setting lets two clusters live on the same office network without ever seeing each other, and mismatched versions announce themselves politely instead of fighting over peers.

The third reason is that your existing tools keep working. Every client you already use targets some API dialect, and the API server mounts adapters for OpenAI Chat Completions, Claude Messages, OpenAI Responses, and Ollama, each translating requests into the cluster’s internal task types and streaming chunks back. Point a coding assistant or a chat frontend at localhost:52415 and the whole cluster answers as if it were one model server. The built-in dashboard at the same port shows live topology, memory, and power per device. The adapters are not thin shims either: tool calls, system prompts, and stream interruption are handled per dialect, and the test suite under src/exo/api/tests covers each contract separately, which tells you the compatibility promise is taken seriously rather than asserted.

The detail view: four API adapters feeding a shared kernel of events and tasks, an elected master running the placement solver, worker engines behind a supervision tree, and the download and discovery infrastructure underneath.

The detail diagram rewards a slow read. On the left, the four adapters in src/exo/api/adapters translate their dialects into typed tasks and publish them onto the zenoh-backed event router, which is the single communication spine every process shares. The master folds each event into state with a pure reducer, consults the cycle solver in placement_utils, and issues PlaceInstance and download commands. On the right, each worker reacts through its local planner, which queues shard downloads first and only then asks the supervisor to spawn a runner. The supervisor tracks acknowledgements, restarts failed runners, and drains cleanly when a new master takes over, which is why you can yank a machine from the cluster mid-request and watch the rest of it carry on. The runner loads the model through the tensor parallel engine, whose model-specific adapters handle DeepSeek, GLM, GPT-OSS, and Gemma variants, while the KV prefix cache makes repeated prompts cheap and batched generation keeps short requests from starving long ones.

Two quieter subsystems deserve attention. The download coordinator tracks a per-shard state machine with verification and cancellation, so a flaky network cannot corrupt weights or strand a half-loaded model. And disaggregated serving splits prefill from decode across machines over a typed wire protocol, an architecture pattern usually reserved for datacenter inference farms. Meanwhile the profilers under src/exo/utils/info_gatherer sample memory, power, and Thunderbolt link health — optionally through the macmon tool — and feed those measurements back into the topology graph, closing the loop that keeps placement decisions grounded in reality rather than in guesses.

From Install to a Running Cluster

On a Mac, the fastest path is the app: brew install --cask exo, launch it, and grant the network-profile prompt so RDMA over Thunderbolt can be enabled on macOS 26.2 or later. From source on macOS or Linux, install uv for Python dependencies, node for the dashboard build, and a stable Rust toolchain, then clone the repository, build the dashboard with npm, run uv sync --extra mlx, and start with uv run exo. Every device that runs that command joins the same cluster automatically; open http://localhost:52415 on any of them to see the merged topology, then send a chat request from any OpenAI-compatible client and watch the shards light up. If you use Nix, nix run .#exo skips most setup entirely, and the Cachix binary cache spares you the Xcode Metal toolchain download.

Honest limits: exo is built around Apple Silicon and the MLX backend, so this is the tool for Macs and Apple-silicon Linux boxes rather than a general CUDA cluster manager; RDMA needs Thunderbolt 5 hardware and a very recent macOS; the dashboard and app are young and still rough around permissions; and clusters are meant for one network segment, not the wide area. None of that dims the educational value: few projects let you watch a distributed system elect, schedule, and infer, all in a couple thousand lines you can actually read.
entry.summary: A guided tour of the exo-explore/exo source tree: how automatic discovery, master election, topology-aware placement, and tensor parallelism run frontier models across ordinary machines.

entry.title: Your AI Second Brain, Self-Hosted - Inside khoj-ai/khoj

link.title: Your AI Second Brain, Self-Hosted - Inside khoj-ai/khoj

entry.content:
Everyone accumulates a private mountain of notes, PDFs, and half-remembered web pages. Khoj is the AGPL-3.0 personal AI that turns that mountain into something you can actually talk to: a self-hostable second brain that ingests your markdown, PDFs, org-mode files, Word docs, Notion pages, and GitHub repos, then lets you chat with any of the major LLMs — local or hosted — about all of it at once. It scales from an on-device assistant to a cloud deployment, reaches you through a web app plus Obsidian, Emacs, desktop, and Android clients, and layers on automations, custom agents, image generation, voice, and even computer-use operators that can drive a browser for you. The README’s benchmark claims are modestly understated; the feature list is not.

Architecturally it is a Django monolith done right: one models file holds every table, format-specific ingestion processors funnel into a shared entry builder, a compact search engine blends embeddings with classic scoring, and a very large helpers module orchestrates whatever tools the conversation needs. Born as an Emacs search package and grown into a full product with a cloud offering, it wears its evolution openly in the source tree. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

Khoj at a glance: a Django server with one shared data model on top, ingestion processors feeding a semantic search core, a conversation brain that grounds answers in your documents, and clients everywhere.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Django entry — the ASGI application that runs migrations and loads ML models in a background thread at startup.
  • The configurator — mounts every router, middleware, and scheduled job when the server boots.
  • The data models — all Django models in one file: users, entries, embeddings, agents, automations.
  • The content processors — format adapters sharing one entry builder that deduplicates, chunks, and diff-updates.
  • The embedder — local or hosted embedding models with vectors cached as compressed binary blobs.
  • The semantic search — blended embedding and tf-idf scoring with optional cross-encoder reranking.
  • The chat helpers — the orchestration core choosing tools, running research, and streaming answers.
  • The deep research loop — an agentic planner that searches, reads, and iterates before responding.

Why You Need This

The first reason is the ingestion design, which solves the boring half of every personal-knowledge project: keeping an index fresh without hammering your sources. Each format adapter in processor/content converts its source into plain text, and the shared entry builder hashes every entry, skips duplicates, and only updates what actually changed when you resync. That incremental diffing is why Khoj can sit on top of a live Notion workspace or a Git repository without re-reading the world on every cycle, and why syncing stays fast even as the corpus grows. The embedder then caches vectors as compressed binary blobs, so restarts are cheap and local-first stays genuinely local.

The second reason is that search here is a masterclass in pragmatism. The semantic search module is barely two hundred lines yet blends vector similarity with tf-idf scores and optional cross-encoder reranking, deliberately avoiding a heavyweight vector database dependency. The date filter parses human phrases like “from: last month” out of natural queries, with sibling filters for file types and exact words. If you have ever wanted to understand how far good engineering, rather than expensive infrastructure, can take retrieval quality, these three files are the case study.

The third reason is the conversation stack’s honesty about providers. The chat helpers — the largest file in the repo — route a single conversation across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and offline models, normalizing tool calls and streaming into one coherent flow. When a question deserves more than one pass, control escalates to the deep research loop, which plans sub-queries, reads sources with visible progress, and iterates until it can answer with citations. A prompt library in processor/conversation/prompts.py keeps every instruction in one auditable place, so you can see exactly what the system tells your models.

The detail view: server and auth at the top, ingestion adapters converging on the entry builder, the search core with its filters, the conversation brain with provider adapters, and the tool belt beside it.

The detail diagram shows a clean funnel. Everything you feed Khoj — markdown, PDF, org-mode, Notion, GitHub — narrows into the entry builder and lands in the single Django models file, which is the whole database in one readable file. The search group reads from those tables, with the three filters composing inline in any query. On the right, the conversation brain fans out: helpers pick tools per turn, the provider adapters speak each vendor’s dialect, and the tool belt ranges from online search to MCP integration, sandboxed code execution, and computer-use operators that drive browser and desktop environments through provider-specific agents. Custom agents in api_agents.py customize persona, knowledge, and model per agent, automations schedule recurring jobs like personal newsletters, and image plus speech generation round out the senses.

The clients group is a reminder of the project’s Emacs roots. The web app is the primary interface today, but the Obsidian plugin and Emacs package query the same API, and the desktop client simply wraps the web experience in an Electron shell. One server, many doors — no per-client logic to drift out of sync, and every interface inherits improvements to search and chat the moment the server updates, which is exactly how a multi-client product should behave.

From Install to a Chat With Your Notes

The official path is Docker: grab the docker-compose.yml from the repository, set your administrator account and one provider key, and docker compose up brings up the server on localhost:42110, where the web app walks you through connecting your first documents. For development, the repo ships a devcontainer and a setup script under scripts that provisions Postgres and all Python dependencies. Once running, upload or connect a folder of notes, wait for the indexing jobs to finish, then just ask a question — Khoj decides whether to answer from your knowledge, search the web, or escalate to deep research, and streams its reasoning as it goes so you are never staring at a silent spinner. Point the Obsidian plugin or the Emacs package at the same server and your second brain follows you into the editor, searchable without breaking your writing flow.

Honest limits: Khoj is AGPL-3.0, which matters if you embed it in a hosted product; the helpers module’s size makes the chat flow harder to follow than the rest of the codebase; self-hosting assumes comfort with Docker and Postgres; and the richest features — automations, computer-use operators, voice — lean on hosted model APIs rather than fully offline setups. The Android client also lags the web experience. Even so, for a readable, end-to-end example of building a personal AI over your own corpus, it remains one of the best codebases to study.
entry.summary: A guided tour of the khoj-ai/khoj source tree: Django server, multi-format content ingestion, semantic search with inline filters, multi-provider chat, deep research, and computer-use operators.

entry.title: MarkItDown: Twenty-Five Converters Behind One MCP Tool - Inside microsoft/markitdown

link.title: MarkItDown: Twenty-Five Converters Behind One MCP Tool - Inside microsoft/markitdown

entry.content:
Ask an LLM to read a PDF and it cannot; ask it to read markdown and it can. That one-sentence gap is why microsoft/markitdown became infrastructure: a small MIT-licensed library that turns documents into markdown, used everywhere from RAG ingestion scripts to coding agents that need to see what is inside a file. What earns it a source tour is the engineering hiding under the plain façade. The core is a dispatch engine barely seven hundred lines long, surrounded by twenty-five converters that each understand one format deeply — Word documents with OMML equations translated to LaTeX, PowerPoint shapes walked slide by slide, Excel sheets rendered as real tables, Outlook message files parsed with attachments, YouTube pages stripped to transcripts. The architecture is a textbook of extension design: one accepts-convert contract, plugins loaded through Python entry points, and an official OCR package that does not fork the converters but subclasses them. And the monorepo ends with a proof of the design’s tightness — the MCP server that gives coding agents access to all of it is one hundred nineteen lines.

The architecture is a monorepo of four packages. The core package holds the MarkItDown class — a converter registry, a source resolver that accepts paths, URLs, data URIs, and streams, and the CLI. The converters live one directory deep, each a self-contained module implementing two methods: accepts, which judges whether it can handle a file based on its stream info, and convert, which does the work. A second ring of converters reaches out to the live web — YouTube, Bing result pages, RSS feeds, Wikipedia — turning network fetches into the same markdown output as local files. The extension packages demonstrate the two extension axes: a sample plugin shows the entry-point mechanism any third party can use, while the OCR package registers subclasses of the document converters so scanned pages get recognized text without touching core code. The MCP package wraps the engine in one tool, with test suites pinning its transport behavior. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

MarkItDown at a glance: the CLI drives the engine, the engine dispatches through the accepts-convert contract to document and web converters, the OCR package upgrades conversion as a plugin, and the MCP server exposes the whole fleet to agents.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The engine routes sources to converters and normalizes the markdown out.
  • The command line wraps the engine with format hints and output options.
  • The converter contract is accepts and convert, nothing more.
  • The PDF converter extracts page by page and defers to plugins for scans.
  • The Word converter maps styles to headings and equations to LaTeX.
  • The image converter reads EXIF and can caption through a vision model.
  • The OCR package subclasses the office converters with a recognition service.
  • The MCP server exposes one tool over stdio, SSE, or streamable HTTP.

Why You Need This

The first reason is the contract, because it is the cleanest small example of plugin architecture in the LLM tooling world. The base converter defines accepts and convert; the engine keeps a list, tries each in order, and raises a clear failure if none accept. The subtlety lives in the inputs: StreamInfo carries mimetype, charset, filename, and extension so accepts can judge without reading the whole file, and the URI helpers classify whether the source is a URL, a local path, or a data URI before anything is fetched. Registration happens three ways — built-in converters registered in the constructor, third-party plugins loaded through Python entry points as the sample plugin demonstrates, and direct register_converter calls for embedding. The result is a library where adding a format never means editing the engine, which is exactly why twenty-five formats coexist without the codebase becoming a swamp.

The second reason is the converters themselves, because they encode years of “what actually matters when a model reads this format.” The Word converter maps Word styles to markdown structure and delegates the genuinely hard parts to helpers: the OMML translator walks Word’s equation XML into LaTeX with a symbol dictionary, and the image extractor emits markdown references for embedded media. The PowerPoint converter walks shape trees and speaker notes so slide decks become readable narratives. The PDF converter keeps its dependency footprint light and offers a plugin upgrade path for scanned pages. On the media side, the image converter pulls EXIF metadata and, when given an LLM client through the caption helper, generates alt-text for pictures no document mentioned — a small feature with outsized value for accessibility and retrieval alike.

The third reason is the extension story, because the OCR package shows how to extend a library without forking it. Rather than modifying the converters, the OCR plugin registers subclasses: the OCR PDF converter extends the original, rasterizes pages, and runs them through a recognition service wrapping a local model, and siblings do the same for Word, PowerPoint, and Excel — each proven by inheritance test suites. The same pattern reaches the cloud through the Document Intelligence converter, which swaps local extraction for Azure’s layout-aware service when you configure an endpoint. The endpoint of this design is the MCP server: because the engine already does everything, the server only maps one tool onto it and selects a transport — one hundred nineteen lines, with transport and error test suites keeping the protocol behavior pinned.

The detail view: the engine with stream info and URI resolution; the document formats with their math and media helpers; media and web converters from images and audio to YouTube and RSS; the extension surface of plugins, OCR and cloud extraction; and the MCP package with its tests.

The detail view shows the dispatch structure plainly. Every converter edge returns to the same base contract — office formats with their helpers on one side, web sources on the other, media in between — so the engine’s dispatch loop is the only place that knows them all. The extension group is visually separate for a reason: plugins, OCR subclasses, and the cloud converter attach at the same seam, meaning the library’s cloud story and its offline story are both “just converters.” The MCP package sits apart and small, wrapping the engine rather than duplicating any of it — the visual argument that clean core architecture makes the protocol layer trivial.

From Install to an Agent-Readable File

Installation is pip install markitdown, and the smallest useful command is markitdown report.pdf > report.md — point it at any supported file and markdown comes out stdout. From there the useful flags are few: -e lists which optional format extensions are enabled, --use-docintel routes PDFs through Azure Document Intelligence when you have an endpoint, and the LLM flags turn on image captioning when you have a vision-capable client. For agents, install the server package — pip install markitdown-mcp — and run markitdown-mcp for the stdio transport your MCP client expects, or add --sse for networked use; a Dockerfile ships for containerized deployments. Programmatically, MarkItDown().convert("file.docx").text_content is the whole API surface most applications need, and enable_plugins in the constructor is the switch that pulls third-party entry-point packages like the OCR one into the registry. Nothing in that flow requires configuration files, credentials, or a running service unless a specific converter — Document Intelligence, transcription, captioning — is used.

Honest limits: this is a converter, not a parser — complex PDF layouts, multi-column academic papers, and heavily designed decks lose fidelity, and the library is honest that its PDF story is text-first with visual extraction delegated to services. The web converters depend on third-party page structures, so YouTube and Bing handling can break when those sites change. OCR runs a local recognition model with its own dependency weight, and the MCP package, while tiny, inherits all of it — install only what you convert. And as with any preprocessor that feeds models, garbage in propagates: the tool’s own guidance is that output should be spot-checked before it becomes a retrieval corpus.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of microsoft/markitdown: the file-to-markdown engine behind countless LLM ingestion flows, its accepts-convert converter contract across PDF, Office, web and media formats, the entry-point plugin system, an OCR package that subclasses the converters themselves, and the 119-line MCP server that exposes it all to coding agents.

entry.title: OpenAI Agents SDK: The Run Loop Beneath the Handoffs - Inside openai/openai-agents-python

link.title: OpenAI Agents SDK: The Run Loop Beneath the Handoffs - Inside openai/openai-agents-python

entry.content:
Most agent frameworks sell you an abstraction and hide the loop.
